* Accrual needs to be corrected from 1.83 per month to 2 days per fully month worked (this means that if one person starts on day 4 of the month, only on day 4 of the following month they get the 2 days of holidays - no 1 day accruals, no decimal accruals)
** This method of accrual needs to be in place during the first full year of contract. 
* Starting on the first civil year after one year tenure, the employee gets automatically 22 days starting on January 1st.
* Regarding *carryover* holidays:
** For people with start date after July of the previous year, carryover days can only be used until 30th of June of the next year.
** For people with start date before that, carryover days can only be used until 30th of April of next year.
** When the year changes, a notification should be sent with the number of carryover days to be booked.
** 2 months before each of these deadlines, the respective employees should receive an automatic notification on the expiry of these days.
* On the first civil year of contract, any employee should have a maximum of 20 days.
* Regarding *unpaid leaves*:
** When trying to book these, a notification should appear if the employee has >0 holiday accrual;
** If someone has unpaid leaves scheduled, an exception needs to be made in the holiday accrual: in the following year, accrual can only be counted for the time worked the previous year (if an employee has a 1-month unpaid leave in 2021, then in 2022 he is only owed 20 days of holidays)
* Holidays booked within the *first 6 months* of contract need to be approved by Manager + People Partner.
* Regarding *overrides:*
** For circumstances where new employees have negotiated booking holidays within the first 6 months, any override changes need to be automatically deducted from the total accrual, including leaving a negative accrual number of holidays. Would that be possible?

My summary for action points:

* {{get-default-instrument}} and {{get-instruments}} should use read-only DB replicas instead of read-write master node to serve requests
* if {{instruments}} are down {{client-commerce-proxy}} should allow {{cash}} and {{bolt  balance}} as an option
* {{isolated instruments}} project is {{critical}} to protect us against incidents like today: independent storage not overlapping with payment services at all
* we should replace {{notifications}} and {{payment-worker}} crons by SNS/SQS to make load balanced over all nodes
* we should split {{card adding}} and {{pre-order}} authorisations into separate tables and guarantee that {{pre-order}} authorisations are not affected, if {{card adding}} attempts have a spike
* we need to have {{auto-scaling}} for number of service nodes (limited to {{2x}} nodes from regular amount), if CPU usage goes >95% for 5 minutes

Hi [~accountid:5de0e80a2c5dd20d0f8ffb6a] - Thanks for your patience on this ticket. Some points:

1) All recruitment agency fees are typically clear as mud in their T+Cs. I anticipate the amount quoted to you is exclusive of VAT, but you may want to check. Ask them to expressly set out any other fees they are intending to charge. Once you’re sure of the position, make sure the fees are OK from a business sign-off perspective.

2) You should clarify how quickly you can dismiss the temps (for convenience) if they aren’t any good, as this isn’t set out clearly in the terms and conditions. Perhaps this has been relayed separately already, but do get them to confirm and make sure you are happy with these timings from a business sign-off perspective. I expect Bolt to be able to give a weeks' notice or similar.

3) Be aware that there will be a steep agency fee if the temps are made permanent (at least 20% of the temp’s annual salary once at Bolt). Do keep this in mind as if the positions become full time, it could be cheaper to hire different persons to avoid these fees. 

4) Make sure the agency knows that the temps are expected to be able to drive… this is obvious but it would be useless to be provided with someone that can’t\!

5) Can you please reach out to [~accountid:6026964fce2bee006a50a166] and check that he is OK with the temps driving our vehicles from an insurance perspective. You should only proceed once [~accountid:6026964fce2bee006a50a166] has confirmed he has no issues.

5) I’m conscious that these temps will be processing personal data. I am going to ask our privacy team to comment on this aspect (to confirm if anything else needs doing).

Otherwise, I’m OK with this proceeding. Please reach out to [~accountid:6026964fce2bee006a50a166] and I will ask the privacy team to comment here. Thanks.

Hi [~accountid:609f85c547ba02006fe1b9c3] - see the main ticket re: using a temp agency.

I’m OK with the arrangement generally, but I note that the temps will be processing personal data. All we have in the recruitment agency contract is this statement:

_“In particular, for the purposes of the Data Protection Act 2018 (“DPA”), both the Client and Reed are data controllers as defined in the DPA and both parties shall comply with their respective obligations under the DPA.”_

When searching regarding this issue, I did find some commentary here (although I think this relates to a more complex scenario than ours): [https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/what-may-compliance-gdpr-require-entities-who-use-from-lazaridis/|https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/what-may-compliance-gdpr-require-entities-who-use-from-lazaridis/|smart-link]

Phone call recording for quality, dispute handling and training purposes will be conducted under the legitimate interest legal basis (GDPR art 6 (1) f). This means that we do not ask consent from the person, but +must inform them about the recording taking place.+ I checked the guidelines from [Finland’s Office of the Data Protection Ombudsman|https://tietosuoja.fi/en/faq-phone-calls#:~:text=Citizens%20have%20the%20right%20to,on%20the%20protection%20of%20communications.] and they align with such practice. They have stated that “_the conversation partner must always be informed of the collection of personal data (incl. recording the call). The manner of this notification is left to the discretion of the controller. The data subject can be informed of the collection of data at the start of the call or earlier, such as in the agreement on which the customer relationship is based.”_ 

# *Informing about the recording* 

Our approach is to inform the caller in the beginning of the call (both inbound and outbound). They should be informed about the following:

a) about the fact of recording;
b) about the purpose of recording.

*2. Retention period*

All personal data processed must have a retention period. No personal data should be kept indefinitely, so a proportionate and reasoned retention time must be set for keeping this data. 

2.1 Retention period must be determined by the local team depending on the purpose why this data is being collected. Data can be stored for no longer than it is necessary for the purposes for which it was collected (e.g the market practice for storing this data is 1 year but can be shorter or longer depending on the need). FYI, support tickets are stored for 3 years (with Beehive this should be 2 years), so the retention period could be aligned with this.

2.2 After the retention period, call recordings must be deleted automatically. 

*3. Data processing agreement*

If there is a third party (service provider) who we use for the technical assistance for recording the call, then we should have a contract in place with them as they would be processing the personal data. 

*Necessity of having phone support in Finland*

In my view, this is not strictly about our liability (yes it can come to that if we are arguing with the driver). But I think first we need to understand if it’s definitely only a case of fraud from the passenger or if the driver was also involved. I am dubious that the ride went on for more than 10 hours without the driver being involved in this fraud. But then if you think that the driver was definitely not involved in the fraud, then there is our strict liability under the T&Cs but there is also our reputation that we need to think of: should we really argue that the driver should not be given the whole amount of the ride when he drove more than 10 hours even if he was acting in good faith and if this is due to our app’s fault? This is what I need to understand so let’s discuss please.

+In the meantime (and to assist during our call), here is what the Belgium T&Cs are saying about Fare calculation errors and about our liability more broadly speaking:+

_FARE CALCULATION ERRORS 4.8._ *_If You find that there has been an error in the calculation of the Fare_* _and wish to make corrections in the calculation of the Fare,_ *_You must immediately submit a request in the section “Fare Review“ of the Bolt App_*_. If such a request has not been submitted_ *_within 24 hours after the Transportation Services were provided_*_, then Bolt shall not recalculate the Fare or reimburse You for an error made in the calculation of the Fare._ 

→ +So strictly speaking, if he didn’t follow that process clearly explained in the T&Cs he signed up to, we are not legally obliged to pay him the missing part of the Fare+…

_SUSPICION OF DRIVER’S FRAUD 4.9. Bolt may adjust the Fare for a particular order completed, if we detect a violation (such as taking a longer route without an express request from the Passenger or not stopping the fare meter of the Bolt App or the taxi meter after the Transportation Services have been completed) or in case a technical error affecting the final Fare is identified._ *_Bolt may also reduce or cancel the Fare in case we have reasonable cause to suspect fraud_* _or gross negligence. Bolt will only exercise its right to reduce or cancel the fare in a reasonable and justified manner._

_MISSING PAYMENT FROM PASSENGER 4.10. Passengers may have the option to pay the Fare for the Transportation Services either directly to the Driver or via the In-app Payment, as described in section 6 of these General Terms. In case the Passenger pays the Fare directly to the Driver, it is the Driver’s obligation to collect the Fare._ *_In case the Passenger fails or refuses to pay, Bolt will send a notice of debt to the Passenger on Your behalf. Such authorisation derives from the mandate of paying agent given to Bolt and does not entail that Bolt has an obligation to compensate the Fare not paid by the Passenger._* _If the passengers in the vehicle do not agree to pay the Fare for the provision of Transportation Service, the Fare will be paid by the Passenger who has ordered the provision of Transportation Service. If Passenger justifiably refuses to pay the Fare on the account that Your information stated in the Bolt App is incorrect, then Bolt will not reimburse You for such expenses._

_6.6. We are not obliged to pay You the Fare due from the Passenger if the In-app Payment failed because the Passenger’s credit card or other payment is cancelled or is unsuccessful for other reasons. In such case we will help You in requesting the Fare due from the Passenger and shall transmit it to You once the Passenger has made the requested payment._

→ This means that +strictly speaking we do not have an obligation to compensate the driver, we only have an obligation to send a notice of debt to the passenger and to help the driver in trying to obtain the Fare+… But let’s discuss this tomorrow please.

_BOLT’S EXCLUSION OF LIABILITY 12.4. We shall not be liable for the actions or non-actions of the Passenger or co-passengers and shall not be liable for any loss or damage that may incur to You, Your Drivers or your vehicle as a result of actions or non-actions of the Passenger or co-passengers._

→ Bolt is not liable for the inaction of the Passenger (such as refusing to pay ) HOWEVER if it appears (or even seem) that the driver is legit and the ride was legit, and our app was faulty / didn’t calculate the correct price, then this is different and our exclusion of liability doesn’t stand in my view.

Maybe there’s a chance that if linter can recognize that it’s a pure metadata change query (adding enum value is the only use case for it so far), then we would have confidence that it can be applied to all runtime schemas both in prelive and live. I can comment on the reason part.

*We’re exploring this to allow us to offer all the options to our potential engineering hires.* Hiring is usually tough, but it is especially tough this year. And we’re not expecting it to get easier anytime soon.

----

In both Romania and Poland, a number of people collaborate via this method. In Poland, about 50% of senior engineering candidates work like this. And in Romania, it is increasing percentage.

The reason is primarily for tax optimization purposes. But there are other benefits too: part-time contracting work for example or more accessible access to some forms of credit.

We are expecting even more of the folks to want to work like this in the future. Many US and Western Europe startups have begun to hire remotely in Eastern Europe. And they hire folks via B2B contracts. They also offer Western rates. Even if we can compete with them on the gross, we can’t on the net.

Regardless _some_ won’t want to work with us even if compensation would be OK, because they’re otherwise tied to their B2B entity.

*The ideal outcome here would be that we enable B2B hiring and we are unblocked on the hiring side by this thing. We don’t want to force people one way or another, just to be flexible with what they want.*

But I’m also OK with us being very clear that we don't want to do this for legal or other reasons.

But right now there are a couple of companies hiring like this (Glovo in Poland, the aforementioned US startups, etc.). And I think our view has been that we’re not doing it because we’ve never done it. Which isn’t ideal.

We need to add a default value for the fields {{taxify_company.scheduled_task.due_time}}

The DB servers has the {{explicit_defaults_for_timestamp}} disabled. This means that {{TIMESTAMP}} columns following the first one, must: *Explicitly allow* {{NULL}} *or have a* {{DEFAULT}} *value.* Otherwise the automatic {{DEFAULT}} is {{'0000-00-00 00:00:00'}}

{noformat}mysql> SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'explicit_defaults_for_timestamp';
+---------------------------------+-------+
| Variable_name                   | Value |
+---------------------------------+-------+
| explicit_defaults_for_timestamp | OFF   |
+---------------------------------+-------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec){noformat}

 

The field {{due_time}}:

* Is not the first {{TIMESTAMP}} type,
* It is declared as {{NOT NULL}}
* and it has no explicit {{DEFAULT}}

So MySQL automatically declared as {{DEFAULT '0000-00-00 00:00:00'}}.

_Please refer to_ [MySQL 5.7 Reference Manual :: sysvar_explicit_defaults_for_timestamp|https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.7/en/server-system-variables.html#sysvar_explicit_defaults_for_timestamp]

 

With this, we hit another restriction:

The {{sql_mode}} in DB servers has includes {{NO_ZERO_DATE}}, which means that the {{DEFAULT '0000-00-00 00:00:00'}} is not a valid value.

{noformat}mysql> SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'sql_mode';
+---------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Variable_name | Value                                                                                                                              |
+---------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| sql_mode      | IGNORE_SPACE,ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY,STRICT_TRANS_TABLES,NO_ZERO_IN_DATE,NO_ZERO_DATE,ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO,NO_ENGINE_SUBSTITUTION |
+---------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec){noformat}

_Please refer to_ [MySQL 5.7 Reference Manual :: SQL Mode :: NO_ZERO_DATE|https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.7/en/sql-mode.html#sqlmode_no_zero_date]

 

An attempt to create the table as described above will fail with the following error: {{ERROR 1067 (42000): Invalid default value for 'due_time'}}

 

Possible solutions are:

# Enable {{explicit_defaults_for_timestamp}}, which requires further analysis, as the database servers are shared hosts and the change will apply to other services.
# Explicitly declare a default non zero value i.e. {{due_time TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP}}.
# Explicitly declared with the {{NULL}} attribute.

*Which are the countries most affected? What is the cause of the random peaks? How can we anticipate them?* 

# *Azerbaijan* - Noticed 43% increase in cash-blocked drivers on the 24th Feb 2022 as they’ve updated their cash-blocking limits from -15 azn to -10 azn. The reason behind this was to decrease the number of drivers with negative balance & explain to keep their balance positive.
# *Ghana* - noticed -49% decrease in cash-blocked drivers on the 4th Dec 2021 from ~15k to ~7.7k blocked drivers. Since then the number of cash-blocking drivers has been slowly increasing again, currently sitting ~12k blocked drivers per day. They’ve increased the limits from -90 to -150 in Accra & from -50 to -100 in Kumasi
# *Kenya* - seeing a lot of jumps in cash-blocked totals but showing slight decrease over time:
## Jumps during the weekend + Cellulant issues during the weekend
# *Nigeria* - similar to Kenya a lot of jumps in totals, the average staying roughly the same at 17k blocked drivers
## Jumps during the weekend + invalid bank information (drivers can’t change this info by themselves)
## Since Jan we’ve introduced Cellulant payment option to Nigeria (switched in March) - the variation in blocked drivers is much smaller
# *Saudi Arabia* - slow increase in total numbers from ~8k to ~11k drivers. Not many huge peaks in numbers but still a few days with 3-4% increase:
## They’ve decreased the limit from -150 to -100 for a couple of companies
# *South Africa* - slight increase in Dec & overall increased ~15k to ~17k drivers in 3 months. Not too much variation in blocked numbers but as said it’s slowly increasing MoM
## Small peaks (+1,+2%) during the weekend
# *Tanzania* - similar story as for the other African countries above - seeing increase in Dec & overall number is slowly increasing
## Peaks during the weekend + Cellulant issues during the weekend
# *Tunisia* - very frequent jumps in number of blocked drivers - weekly on the weekends. But although we’re seeing this variation they’re paying back hence the total number of blocked drivers is roughly the same across the 3 months
# *Uganda* - sitting around 8k blocked drivers per day, not many jumps (although we’ve experienced issues with Cellulant during the time period - the outages didn’t affect much)
# *Ukraine* - jump on 26th Feb 
## War with Russia

*How do we change limits accordingly?*

I took 2 examples: Azerbaijan (where we’ve made the limit more strict on the 24th Feb 2022) & Ghana (where we’ve increased the blocking limit on the 4th Dec 2021) to see how the markets are performing before & after the change.

In Azerbaijan we saw 18% (+60k eur per day) increase in GMV & 10% (+17k rides per day) increase in total rides after the update whereas the increase in total drivers wasn’t that large - noticed 2% (+3k per day) increase in total drivers. Also noticed an increase in Online Hours: +4% (4k per day) & in average number of rides per driver: +8% (+0.5 rides per driver). Of course, the total debt increased (+385%) after the update as there were 50% more drivers cash-blocked in a day but interestingly the % change in total debt slowed down after decreasing the blocking limits - from -0.85% per day (before) to -0.59% per day (after). Noticed +33% increase in CS tickets on driver debt after the limits were changed. In general we do see a slight declination in cash-blocked drivers (sitting around 31k currently) but it’s still far from the number before the change (23k before). Drivers in total have more debt (which is covered due to increase in OH, GMV, rides) but the main goal of decreasing debt isn’t working as quickly as expected - the drivers aren’t paying as much to decrease their overall debt & opening up more tickets to Bolt (which isn’t the best solution long-term)

In Ghana we’ve noticed +11% in GMV (+42k eur per day) after the blocking limits were increased but the number of rides stayed the same & the number of active drivers decreased by 2% (-400 drivers per day). Also the OH decreased by 4% (-4k per day) & driver payments dropped -25% after the limit was loosened. As expected the total debt from the cash-blocked drivers have increased by 43% & the % change for debt accelerated after the update - there’s more room for drivers to accumulate negative balance. Which comes to the CS tickets, there’s 30% decrease in tickets on driver debt. In general we noticed a huge decrease in cash-blocked drivers after the change (from 15k to 8k) but as it’s been a few months the numbers are slowly creeping up to the same level currently being at ~13k blocked drivers per day. The drivers are accumulating more debt & I don’t think increasing the limit for all drivers is the best solution to generate more GMV (as we see the OH & rides per driver decreased). 

Better solution would be something between the 2 - we update the limits more frequently (e.g. if there’s an issue with Cellulant we make the limit larger & if everything’s running as usual we keep quite strict limits to deny drivers accumulate debt). Another idea would be fluid limits on a driver level - good drivers have larger limit & vice-versa but not sure how can we incorporate it into fee calculator.

*March 16 update:*

We had a meeting with the Risk & Safety team (Anni Faltis) and Drive OPS (Henriko Aer, Maksim Palonen). The following questions were discussed:

* How do we currently discover potential fuel theft cases - does it come from OPS or CS?
* When do we consider the fuel card being stolen?
* How should we communicate with the user who is the potential fuel thief?
* Do we need to block the rental if there is no fuel card and no fuel?
* When do we block the user? Do we hard-block them or allow them to use other services?

All points were discussed and further action items confirmed - the checklist was updated according to what we agreed on.

----

*Discovering potential fuel cases*
Almost all fuel theft cases come from the OPS team - it isn’t CS who discover them. There may be a few reported cases where the reporter had seen someone with a Drive vehicle putting fuel into a canister. However, regular users pretty much do not care about someone stealing fuel. It is up to OPS to discover these potential fuel thieves.
The OPS team checks if the vehicle had been actually refuelled. Photos are taken when needed. We contact the customer and observe their behaviour.

*When do we consider the fuel card stolen?*
If CS escalate to OPS that a fuel card is missing from a car, OPS look for the customer who might have taken the fuel card with themselves. This customer is contacted and asked if the fuel card might be with them - if yes, then this is not considered fuel card theft. 
OPS cannot see the last time the fuel card was used - however, they can check when a vehicle was last refuelled using this card.

*How should we communicate with the potential fuel thief?*

* Our message should always be that “we have a suspicion that their account was used to steal the fuel” - we don’t want to accuse the user that they stole the fuel
* Any communication must be done by Tier 2 CS (Stealing Fuel is also a Significant risk type event)
* OPS don’t want to share data on specific amounts of fuel stolen or any other data like that with the accused user and also with the CS
* Any tickets with users asking why they received a criminal charge for fuel theft (or however the police forms the charge), only Tier 2 CS agents should handle these cases
* If more questions are asked, the response should be along the lines of "unfortunately, we cannot provide any further details at this moment. Any communication will come from the police"
* We always want to separate Bolt from the punisher (in this case, the police since there will be a criminal charge for theft)
* Relevant comments must be left on the user profile page in Admin (by Tier 2) and the OPS Case Manager (Maksim) should be looped in, too

*Do we need to block the rental?*
The Global Event Assessment Tool currently asks to block the rental in case of the Stealing Fuel HP event. However, OPS confirmed that there is no need to hide the vehicle - the Fleet OPS Specialists react quickly (within 45-60 min) and refuel the car within minutes. This is true for smaller cities like Tallinn. Additionally, even if there’s no fuel card in the car, the users can refuel the vehicle themselves and then reach out to us to coordinate the refund.
For larger cities, it may take more time for the Fleet OPS Specialists to react and refuel the car. However, OPS can adjust the minimum fuel level for the vehicles in these cities from which the vehicle will automatically be hidden.

Anni will adjust the Assessment Tool to not require blocking the rental.

*Do we hard-block the user or allow them to use other Bolt services?*
OPS have observed that users who are potential fuel thieves also have bad behaviour characteristics when using Bolt Food (requesting refunds for minor issues, mixups) - so we can block them on all platforms. This is supported by the Risk & Safety team, as well as the Legal team.

*Solving the OPS issue, not wasting time on investigations*

❗ Henriko explained that the issue to resolve is mainly the procedure of refuelling the cars. It is the operational fault that it is so easy for users to steal the fuel cards and therefore also steal the fuel. We should come up with a better process for this. Currently, the investigations take up a lot of resources on multiple teams.

# I prepare a build
# SRE stop the services to take off the load on db
# DBA perform their magic for renaming and setting new permissions and proxysql configs
# SRE restart the current version (not a new one), and everything should work well, because the service will use a new schema by proxysql settings
# After all actions, I deploy a new version and merge release pr (just to fix the new version in the code and for configless stuff)

Please find below answers to your questions.

# That is correct. Since Bolt is going to issue itself invoices in the name and on behalf of the supplier, there needs to be some agreement between them i.e. at least the supplier’s approval. I believe it can be stipulated in the T&C that by accepting the T&C the supplier gives their approval to Bolt to self-issue in the name and on behalf of the supplier. I think that Portugal's example is OK.
# The Fiscalization of invoices is necessary only in case of the payments in cash. |As mentioned in the external advisor's opinion - cash, cards, check, transfer accounts, others are considered to be cash.

Regarding the invoice payment, there should be a clear distinction between the transfer account and the giro account, especially when we are talking about small trade business/craft. A transaction account is the owner's personal account that is not controlled or tracked by tax authorities, and a giro account is their business account that tax authorities can track. For this reason, in case the payment is made on a translation account the invoice must be fiscalized (this transaction is considered to be paid in cash) and in the case, it is made on a giro account it does not need to be. 

Please note that in Croatia any small trade business/craft must have a giro account.

I hope this helps. :) 

Should you have any questions, feel free to ask. 

Best regards,

Taking this all together - there are different purposes on why we would be collecting this data and how we will use it. Different purposes mean different legal basis for processing the data, that’s why it is important to know the exact purpose beforehand. 

I also understand that womens only category is something that we will introduce in the future, right now our goal is to identify the gender for analytics and personalised comms/offers purpose. 

So: 

# *Analytics about the ratio of the women on the platform.* We can add the gender identification “box” to the registration form. E.g. there is a choice between women, man, i don’t wish to answer. Legal basis for the purpose of collecting this data for analytics would be legitimate interest. We can also ask this from our already existing drivers for the same purpose. 
# *Personalised comms for women riders.* This activity means that we are carrying out profiling - placing a person into a certain category according to their characteristics and sending personalised content. This activity would require +data subject’s consent+ for receiving such personalised comms. 
# *Women only category.* As we would be relying on the data gathered in the past for analytical purposes (the gender data provided on registration), then we should ask consent whether the driver agrees that the data will be used for a new purpose. E.g. if such functionality goes live, we ask consent whether they agree with us using the submitted gender information for offering services in the womens only category. 

*On riders side:*

The described solution:

_Can we instead offer the rider to “opt-in” to the Women Drivers category and ask them to:_

_-- provide a reason between:_

* _I’m a woman_
* _I book for another woman or kids_

*Investigate why NG has 3 tiers of blocking*

Different cities have different limits e.g. in Lagos (which is the biggest city in NG & the first city Bolt launched; limit -10k) so the trust is there, and the number of trips the drivers do meaning the drivers easily hit the threshold faster, surge is more because of the number of active rides also impacting how fast drivers hit the threshold etc. We cannot use the same limit that we use in Lagos for Benin (which has the -8k limit) or Uyo, Uyo for example (limit -4k), is still a relatively new city for Bolt and the drivers haven't been on the platform for a long time, there aren’t that many trips and surge wouldn't be high (takes longer for drivers to hit the max limit). Due to the high surge in December, the volume of drivers getting blocked for cash increased in some of the cities. The payment team was overwhelmed because drivers were paying commission debt but the turnaround time to match this payment kept increasing, when we reviewed the threshold higher, it was lower than what it is right now (plans to dial back as Cellulant was rolled out in NG).

*How are debt limits calculated today in the 5 markets; NG, Kenya, ZA, Saudi Arabia, Azerbaijan (see LIMIT = - av_num_rides * av_price * basic_fee * (1- compensation_ratio))*

The cash-block threshold varies by the size of the market (GMV and Rides). The 2 parameters depend on ASP (average surge period) and RPH (rides per hour) of the city. Or in other words, how long does it take a driver to get cash-blocked in any of the cities feeds into the cities threshold. Initially the formula was used to set up the limits but overtime the limits have changed as per CM/OPS requests. Previously, Yury confirmed all updates and now Maret verifies it to avoid any errors.

*Investigate why Saudi has a different unblocking limit (0) compared to other countries which are half of the blocking limit*

They’ve been playing around with the limits quite a bit in the past few months, the latest update being on the 17th Jan where the limit was finalised to -100 / -50. Now Saudi Arabia is following the standard: x = cash blocking limit & x/2 = cash unblocking limit.

Hello, 

My understanding is that there are differences between being a voluntary registered sponsor and a recognised sponsor. I assume Bolt is going for the voluntary alternative.

The legal obligations on sponsors (regardless if voluntary registered or recognised) are several, please see below.

# Bolt must keep the following information about the employee in its records: 

* The employment contract, the appointment decision or the hosting agreement.
* The original work permit (if required) or the additional document accompanying the single permit (GVVA).
* A copy of the passport.
* In the case of a transfer of the employee within a group of companies: a statement from the foreign (parent) company and a statement from the business unit in the Netherlands.
* The payslips.

Bolt must also keep the following information about the employee in its records: 

* The antecedents certificate, completed and signed by the foreign national (only if there is no antecedents).

Sometimes other documents must be included in the administration. This depends on the employee's purpose of residence in the Netherlands. Bolt have a duty to keep records and an obligation to retain. Bolt must retain records and documents for up to 5 years after the sponsorship has ended. The information may also be kept digitally. Bolt must also provide this information when the IND (Immigration and Naturalisation Service in Netherlands) requests it.

2. Bolt must provide information on all relevant changes regarding the employee and its sponsorship:

Bolt is obliged to report changes to the IND if such changes will affect the employee's right of residence. Bolt must report the information within 4 weeks after the fact, circumstance or change occurred. For example, the following information must be reported:

* The employee no longer comes to the Netherlands.
* The employee no longer works for Bolt.
* The employee no longer meets the income requirement or no longer has sufficient, long-term and independent means of support.
* The employee is no longer staying in the Netherlands or Bolt no longer know where the employee is.
* A change of Bolt’s address.
* A change to Bolt’s legal status.
* A change to Bolt’s business purpose.
* Termination of the Bolt company or its operations.
* The fact that criminal proceedings were instituted against one of the managing or executive directors of Bolt.
* Suspension of Bolt’s payment capacity or bankruptcy.
* A merger or acquisition regarding Bolt.
* Having changed contact persons within Bolt.
* Having changed the authorised/legal representative that submits applications on Bolt's behalf.

Furthermore, Bolt is responsible for the foreign national's return. If the foreign national don’t return to his country of origin and there is a compulsory departure enforced by the Dutch government, the IND may oblige Bolt to pay the costs of the compulsory departure.

The IND supervises Bolt’s sponsorship and if Bolt fails to comply with the legal obligations, the IND may impose various sanctions:

* A warning and an administrative penalty.
* Suspension of the recognition as sponsor.
* Withdrawal of the recognition as sponsor.
* Withdrawal of the residence permit.
* Recovery of the costs for the foreign national's removal.

Hi Krisina\!

Regarding the question about travel expenses, please find below our external counsel’s answer:


First of all, it is necessary to define a „_business trip_“. According to Section 42 of the Labour Code, a business trip means "_a time-limited posting of an employee by an employer to perform work outside the agreed place of work_". Therefore, if your employees work outside the place of work specified in their employment contracts, then these are business trips and follow the relevant rules. In the case of some employees, the place of work may be determined broadly (e.g. Czech district or region) and then it is not a business trip if they perform work within this place of work.

The employer may send the employee on a business trip for the time necessary only on the basis of an agreement with him, and the employee on the business trip then performs the work according to the instructions of the employer who sent him on a business trip. The said agreement may be made orally or tacitly so that the employee embarks on a business trip. In practice, the consent is usually provided by the employee signing a so-called „_travel order_“, thus giving consent to posting him on a business trip. The advantage of signing a travel order is that the employee's consent to posting can be traced back, thus avoiding various doubts in future.

I enclose a sample travel order in the attachment to see what it may look like in practice. This sample document contains all the necessary information, including a statement of the costs that the employee had in connection with the business trip. Section 153 of the Labour Code further stipulates: “_Conditions that may affect the provision and amount of travel compensation, in particular the time and place of departure and termination of the trip, the place of performance of work tasks, the mode of transport and accommodation, shall be determined in advance by the employer in the written form; it shall take into account the legitimate interests of the employee. If the employee's rights to travel compensation and their amount are unquestionable, the previous written form of determination of the travel conditions is not required if the employee does not insist on it._” Travel compensation should therefore be discussed in advance. It follows from the cited text that a written form is not necessary, but I recommend it (the attached travel order can also be used for this). 

The employer is therefore obliged to determine the conditions of the business trip, which include, for example, the mode of transport to the business trip, its beginning and end, the methods of accommodation, catering and so on. The employer must then inform the employees about these conditions. The employer should also ensure the safety of work on the given business trip. If an employee becomes injured on a business trip, it can be considered a work-related injury, which can have significant consequences for you. Therefore, it is necessary to include business travel matters in your employee training in the field of occupational safety. In this matter, I recommend that you turn to a professional in the field of occupational safety, who also deals with occupational safety on business trips. He will explain to you how to ensure the maximum safety of your employees and ensure their proper training in this field.

It is also important how to report the activities of employees on a business trip in accounting. From a legal point of view, according to § 210 of the Labor Code, "_time spent on a business trip other than performing work tasks is considered an obstacle to work on the part of the employer. Wages are not reduced for this time_." Which I assume is not very telling for you and you would be more interested in the practical implications. I therefore recommend that you contact your accountants regarding the payment of salaries during the business trip - they will have experience with this issue and will explain the practical aspects of charging wages during the business trip.

The employer is obliged to provide the following compensations to the employee for the business trip:

* Compensation for food (payment to compensate catering of your employee)

* Travel expenses (payment to compensate travel costs of your employee)

* Travel expenses to visit a family member (payment to compensate travel expenses for a family member's visit in the event of longer business trips of your employee)

* Accommodation expenses (self-explanatory)

* Compensation for foreign food (payment to compensate catering of your employee in the event of foreign business trip)

* Additional expenses required (payment to compensate additional costs like parking, highway tolls etc.)

Each of these types of travel compensations concerns a different range of compensated costs and each has its own rules. Again, I recommend working with your accountants to explain how these compensations are applied and accounted for - this is part of the normal day-to-day agenda, so I don't expect them to have a problem. If you would like a more detailed analysis, let me know and I will prepare it.

Travel compensations must be billed - a sample travel order that I send can be used for this. Sheet 2 of the excel file is used to report the costs incurred by the employee according to their type - the employer then reimburses these stated and proven costs.

Hey, Roberts\! 

I wasn’t aware that the process ends up with only changing the status of account and nothing (ever) gets deleted. This is a non-compliance with regulatory requirements. 

As a rule, the account holder does not have to give any reason why they wish to have their account or personal data deleted. This is their right under the GDPR. 

Account deletion should mean that the account can not be retrieved - so the account would be archived (not only closed/status changed). Account deletion should trigger the deletion of personal data (after a period which is set beforehand in the retention schedule). For couriers the retention times are set in the BF [privacy policy.|https://static.food.bolt.eu/legalDocument/bolt_food_privacy_policy_en.pdf] 

Also, if the courier asks for the deletion of their account, then this constitutes as the termination of their agreement with Bolt.

I think there has been so far no archival process nor analysis on how the courier account deletion should take place. I suggest (as an exception in this case) ask the tech support and of the engineers to archive properly this account so that this doesn’t escalate. 

Liis

[~accountid:5f1a8e14e5efc1001bf8ec6d] , we have standard bunch of questions in servicedesk form. please, answer them for each of listed tables:



• Is the table mutable (i.e. existing rows can be updated) or it's immutable/append-only (no row delete, no row update)?

• Does table already have production data? If table is empty (or contains only test data) please provide a strong reason why replication should be set up now, not when actual data are there.

• Why do you need these tables in Redshift?

• Should it be available in Looker?

• Does it contain Personally Identifiable Information (PII) like names, surnames, emails, phone numbers, *users/dirvers/couriers comments/notes*, addresses, etc? Generally PII is information relating to natural persons who can be identified or who are identifiable, directly from the information in question or who can be indirectly identified from that information in combination with other information. If so, it will be replicated to `pii` schema (if it's mutable) or to `ext_pii` schema (if it' s immutable)

• How are you going to use this data? (investigation, build a dashboard, model, etc)

• Do you need historical data too? If yes - since which date exactly? (no need to answer for immutable data - we don't support it)

• Which columns have to be replicated? (Answer "all" or provide list of columns).

• Is any of the columns in JSON format and it also has to be replicated? If so, please list them and explain why do you need them. By default we don't replicate JSONs to Redshift.

• If there any free-style text column such as description, comment, etc? We usually do NOT replicate these columns, please confirm and explain the reason that you need these columns.

• What is the most used column (a.k.a. foreign key) in JOIN (if this table joins other tables)?

•Is this replication for a one-time investigation?

Hi Armin,

as discussed on our call today, I’m following up with a summary of our suggested approach.



We’d suggest to have separate privacy set ups for ride-hailing and for Bolt4Business purposes.

Bolt4Business:

We perceive this data transfer as a controller-to-controller relationship. This role allocation is aligned with the business set up, as our partner will be a contracting party to B4B agreements and it will be demonstrating its own purposes of processing. In this scenario the liability in terms of the Bolt4Business subset of the data personal data lies with our partner.

Ride-hailing:

As the underlying service is provided by Bolt and our partner is providing operational assistance, we see that as a controller-to-processor relationship. This means that ultimately Bolt “owns“ the data and the data subject to this data transferred cannot be repurposed by our partner for other purposes than providing us with operational support. It is also aligned with the role allocation as Bolt is responsible for the platform, infrastructure and its security.  

Suggestions re contract:

* it would be recommended to add “Data Protection“ clause into our contract stipulating that for Bolt4Business purposes the partner and Bolt are acting as separate data controllers in accordance with security instructions and applicable data protection legislation (each of the party is responsible for its own compliance) ;and for ride-hailing purposes, the data processing agreement applies, which should form an annex to the partnership agreement;
* as for the data processing agreement- please see our standard DPA terms here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1l_3q_2QXzXy-zBTWAuB_P4r0f58EFyYkV1iMjnBOa1Q/edit?usp=sharing|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1l_3q_2QXzXy-zBTWAuB_P4r0f58EFyYkV1iMjnBOa1Q/edit?usp=sharing|smart-link]

_Dear Abisola,_ 

_Thank you for raising this issue. In the ticket you are mentioning, the regulator requested the personal data of drivers operating on the bolt platform (phone numbers, vehicle and vehicle plate number), but in the provided letter (14_^_th_^ _march, 2022) the Lagos State Government is asking “for the total number/data of e-Hailing Vehicles/Drivers that logged on the app”:_

*Summary:*

From a data protection point of view, the transmission of the aggregated number of drivers _(without additional descriptive information)_ is unproblematic (it should also be sufficient for the stated purpose). Personal data of drivers must not and cannot be transmitted because the request is not specific enough.

An assessment of whether personal data must be transmitted cannot be made according to the current status, as at least the following information is missing:

# description of the requested data
# description of a legal basis
# comprehensible description of the purpose

*Additional questions:*

# Did they specify what data they want (you mention phone numbers,…)? If yes, please provide details.
# Are you aware of any legal obligation to transmit data in connection with the regulation of taxi or ride hailing services (Is there a taxi and/or ride hailing act or regulations Nigeria)?

*Further explanation*

* +*_Number of Vehicles/Drivers:_*+ _Due to the aggregation and the amount of drivers, the release of the mere number of drivers (without additional descriptive information) appears unproblematic from a data protection point of view because it is not personal data. (The Nigeria Data Protection Regulation describes “Personal Data” as any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person)_
* +*_Additional Data of Drivers/Vehicles:_*+ _In the letter you mention that you are looking for the disclosure of personal data such as telephone numbers, vehicle make and license plate number. This cannot be inferred from the document. Is there any additional correspondence here? If so, I kindly ask for additional information._

_Paragraph 2.2. of the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation requires that personal data only be processed in accordance with_ *_specific, legitimate and lawful purpose_*_. This requires an exact description of the personal data, the legal basis and the purpose._

_Based on the very bold description of the requested data and the vague description of the purpose, a transmission of personal data would be not allowed, considering the provisions of the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation and the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation Implementation Framework 2020. In addition, there is also the fact that no corresponding legal basis can be identified or that it has not been transmitted by the Lagos State Government._

Hi\! 

All these providers are connected to a courier fraud scheme where couriers put a delivery address that generates a long route and gets paid a lot without even having to make the delivery. 

These 6 providers together had 1434 orders delivered in under 1 min, where avg order price was ~6.8 eur and the avg courier earning was ~20.5 eur, a total of 29.3k paid out in courier earnings. Most of the volume came in the week between 07-13/03, 960 orders, 22k euros. 

As Mark highlighted already in Slack and in a previous escalation, we’re already aware of this courier scheme and this will be resolved once the delivery fee calculation changes from a straight line to the actual route. Until then, we’re taking manual action. 

This scheme is majorly on the courier side, but it’s possible that providers get involved, where they would receive a share of the profits without even having to deliver/prep any food. However, this can’t be proved from the data alone. You can check on Looker dashs to see preparation time from these providers, but even then, it’s possible that the products are types of products that are already ready or can be in seconds, such as a Croissant or a Coffee, for example. How can we know exactly how much time does it take for the restaurant to prep a specific item on the menu? How can we know the stock they already have ready or that can be ready in seconds? The list of ordered goods and their preparation time is something that is out of our scope atm, so we wouldn’t advise taking any action on the providers unless you received direct reports from couriers and wish to look into that part in more detail.

h3. Feedback from Safety Team

From our end the suggestion would be to always ask for security questions and actually check that information before giving out any information about Bolt Drive vehicles. As an example, we also wouldn't give out Bolt Office address to a random caller who is not our employee if there is no walk-in.This would have to be monitored by the team leads as it's a [global standard procedure|https://support.taxify.eu/hc/en-us/articles/360008802080--Inbound-phone-call-script]. Perhaps more specific information is needed to the inbound call procedure in case of Bolt Drive trips, or creating a completely separate script which'd be Bolt Drive specific.If a user calls in that they can not locate the vehicle, the first thing to do would be to eliminate user error by:

* asking for their account information to locate the account;
* security questions to understand they are the owner of the account;
* identifying that they are actually able to book a vehicle (checking the user's driving license); and
* that they have reserved the vehicle with the car reg number in question.

If the user provides this information, security questions match, the driving license is present on the user's profile and they have actually reserved this vehicle, only then can we give out information pertaining to the trip, which is vehicle location. Even if the person is calling in and referring to a specific vehicle by car reg number, we shouldn't give out any information about the location of the vehicle before we've done our due diligence.The above would be a preventative measure.As for if the vehicle has been hijacked, the agents should log the event as {{Third Party Hijacked or Attempted Hijack of Vehicle}} in the Assessment Tool as per the [high priority workflow|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3753411849/Carsharing+Safety+Event+Assessment+and+Investigation+Workflow], escalate it to OPS and then OPS would file a report with the police as per their current processes. From the agent's side, if a vehicle is stolen with duplicated keys, it would be difficult to identify which user is at fault and gave the keys to a third party to be duplicated, therefore the investigation would be up to the police and the tool should be closed based on OPS feedback on this case.Please let me know if you have any other questions\!

Hey, the problem for [~accountid:6012aaf8a41ea5006a613a63] and me is to identify charges to users from other countries (except Germany). We are able to match the credit card details that the police give us to users but sometimes 5-10 users from different countries can be matched to the same credit card. The police also send us bank statements, so we would be able to match the exact charges to the user who really misused the credit card. This is when we need help from cs-global. If we know where the fraudulent user comes from we can tag the flag of the country and ask someone to identify the charges to the user to be 100% sure that this user misused the credit card. However, sometimes we don't know where the user comes from and we ask for help in cs-global without tagging a flag. This is when it becomes more difficult because theoretically, all agents need to check if they can find the charges. We had cases where the fraudulent user came from Finland or Montenegro where Bolt does not operate yet. Thus, we were not able to tag a country in cs-global.

* Laptops and phones are in the scope of the termination agreement and such assets will be listed in the transfer agreement. Ownership of the assets is transferred to Bolt. Therefore - in general I don’t see any concerns with the mere fact of taking these assets.

* Do we have a ground and purpose to audit/go through the content of the devices?  The legal basis for this would be legitimate interest. Our legitimate interest - identify the infringement of the obligation to keep the business secret or agreement on non-compete. Maybe also some clauses from our partner agreement can support this etc. Also, we already have information from previous audits of suspicious downloads - which gives us a reason to suspect wrongdoings on a larger scale. So I do believe we have a legitimate interest ground here to argue if we need to conduct audits. 

All in all:

c) BUT -> before any possible information found is used as an evidence/presented to the partner for “breaking the wrist” (as many times mentioned) - let's pause and think if that really serves the purpose. It may result in a risk of opening a pandora box for legal disputes from these employees accusing us of going through their personal information stored on these computers. I’ve analysed different possible reasons of the cron slow-down and have not been able to find a definite reason.

Some background info: 

* there were no code and configuration changes lately in {{invoicing-user}} which could potentially affect the {{PayoutCron}}
* it has been suggested initially that difference in data can potentially be the reason of the slow-down. However, I couldn’t explain the difference in {{cron run}} slow-down by potential data difference. Even if there would be more clients which would require payouts to be generated, it would lead to total cron run to be increased (as in - more rows processed); what has been observed however, was time increase of _each_ cron run (total processing time for each limited dataset)  

My initial idea to reason about slow-down was to check database queries involved in cron process. I’ve created a consolidated table of average times of queries (found from pmm2 dashboards) which are called during payout generation, and did it for 21.03, 14.03 and 28.02 dates (all Mondays) - see screenshot attached and document itself. Significant difference in one the heavy queries ({{getIncomesMinusNegatives}} - it executes multiple {{UNION ALL}} query) made me think that it is a culprit. However, it turned out that the same query slow-down has been observed on Feb 28th but without cron slow-down.

Judging by the variation of query performance and stability of cron times over the March and February I got a strong impression that query times have actually very small impact over cron times.

Next idea which I tried was to verify if there were no issues with network latency between servers and database. This is not a directly observable metric AFAIK, however I made an assumption that increased network latency/decreased network throughput would affect _all_ or at least some other crons running in {{invoicing}} package against mysql {{invoicing}} cluster. However, I’ve not identified any other cron slow-down on March 21st compared to performance of crons on March 14th, except for {{PayoutCron}}. Specifically, {{BalanceCalculationCron}}, quite heavy one, performed in the same manner as it did in the past.

Additional discussions with Boris, former billing EM, uncovered that this issue has been observed in the past, however explorations have not been successful. This problem did happen sporadically, w/o understandable reason.

The framework agreement for the supply of temporary workers by DEKRA Arbeit GmbH essentially corresponds to standard framework agreements for the supply of temporary workers and to the legal requirements of the German Temporary Employment Act (Arbeitnehmerüberlassungsgesetz). The framework agreement does not contain any significant risks that would prevent it from being signed.

In one or two places, however, it does not seem to me to be in line with the interests at stake. Here Bolt should try to adjust the regulations in the framework agreement. In general, temporary employment in Germany is heavily regulated by the German Temporary Employment Act (Arbeitnehmerüberlassungsgesetz), whereby the framework agreement complies with the legal requirements. DEKRA Arbeit GmbH has the necessary permit to supply temporary workers, which is evidenced by Annex 1 of the framework agreement.

The specifications in § 3 of the framework agreement are likely to be correct with regard to Bolt Services DE GmbH. The special obligations of Bolt in § 9 of the agreement correspond to the legal requirements and reflect these accurately. The scope of liability in § 12 also corresponds to the legal requirements. *In the case of temporary employment, the temporary employment agency is only liable for the proper selection of the temporary employee and not for any breaches of duty on the part of the temporary employee*. The background to this is that the temporary worker is subject to the instructions of the client and not the agency during his temporary assignment. According to the framework agreement, *the liability of DEKRA Arbeit GmbH is also limited to gross negligence and intent*, which is, however, quite common in business dealings.

der Rahmenvertrag zur Arbeitnehmerüberlassung der DEKRA Arbeit GmbH entspricht im Wesentlichen gängigen Rahmenverträgen zur Arbeitnehmerüberlassung und den gesetzlichen Vorgaben des Arbeitnehmerüberlassungsgesetzes. Der Rahmenvertrag enthält keine wesentlichen Risiken, die einer Unterzeichnung entgegenstehen.

Die DEKRA Arbeit GmbH hat die notwendige Erlaubnis zur Arbeitnehmerüberlassung, welches durch die Anlage 1 des Rahmenvertrags belegt ist.

Die besonderen Pflichten von Bolt in § 9 des Vertrags entsprechen den gesetzlichen Vorgaben und geben diese zutreffend wieder. Auch der Umfang der Haftung in § 12 entspricht den gesetzlichen Vorgaben. Bei der Arbeitnehmerüberlassung haftet der Verleiher nur für die ordnungsgemäße Auswahl des Leiharbeitnehmers und nicht für etwaige Pflichtverletzungen seitens des Leiharbeitnehmers. Hintergrund ist, dass der Leiharbeitnehmer während seines Einsatzes den Weisungen des Entleihers und nicht des Verleihers unterworfen ist. Laut dem Rahmenvertrag ist die Haftung der DEKRA Arbeit GmbH zudem auf grobe Fahrlässigkeit und Vorsatz beschränkt, welches jedoch im geschäftlichen Verkehr durchaus üblich ist.

*1. Summary - Recommendations:*

* Bolt should offer a Link to a proper privacy notice on the Main-Page and the used application form (first draft in 2.2).
* Instead of including data protection information in the terms and conditions, I would recommend using a separate privacy notice (provide link in the terms and conditions)
* In order to determine who is the controller, it should be clearly defined in advance who is responsible for the action (who decides on the purpose and the chosen means or whether a contest is happening at all) (Bolt Operations ÖU or Bolt Services DE GmbH).
* After the Schrems II decision and the current rulings of multiple data protection authorities regarding the usage of Google services i highly recommend to check if there are other privacy compliant options inside the European union (and use them).
* The company should use a double opt-in to obtain consent. In order to effectively enable a withdrawal of consent, confirmation notifications with the possibility of withdrawal should also be sent to the data subject.

*2. Art. 13-Information:*

*2.1. General remarks*

Where personal data relating to a data subject are collected from the data subject, the controller shall, at the time when personal data are obtained, provide the data subject with all the necessary information. The information has to be provided in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language. 

*→ To hide this information in a multiple page long terms and conditions- document is not GDPR compliant. Bolt should offer a Link to a proper privacy notice on the Main-Page and the used application form.*

Since Bolt also obtains the consent of the data subject before processing, the information provided in advance and the request for consent must be made in an understandable and easily accessible form using clear and plain language.

*→ More about data subject consent in 6.2.*

The controller shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing of his or her personal data. So before the data subject sends their consent, this should be clearly documented by an opt-in field. 

The wording

* _„Mit dem Absenden des Formulars bist du mit der Verarbeitung der persönlichen Daten und den Bedingungen der Kampagne einverstanden.“/"By submitting the form, you agree to the processing of personal data and the terms of the campaign."_ 

seems not sufficient because this consent was given uninformed and therefore is invalid. The following is recommended: 

* _"Ich habe die Datenschutzerklärung (Link) gelesen und stimme der Datenverarbeitung zu."/"I have read the privacy notice (link) and give my consent to the data processing"._

*2.2. Draft „Privacy Notice (*[*https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zo6LWVJhcaywt4LuDKw51mCrB9ZWEp2R/edit*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zo6LWVJhcaywt4LuDKw51mCrB9ZWEp2R/edit]*)*

_Since there are some questions about the used application-form and the collected personal data, I would not recommend using it without adding the missing content (data used, data transfer US, safeguards, ...)._

The notice has to provide the following information:

* purposes of the processing; 
* categories of personal data concerned; 
* recipients or categories of recipient to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed (also recipients in third countries or international organisations)
* period for which the personal data will be stored (if not possible, the criteria used to determine that period)
* existence of the right to request from the controller rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning the data subject or to object to such processing
* right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority; 
* where data are not collected from the data subject, any available information as to the source;
* information about the appropriate safeguards (where data are transferred to a third country or to an international organisation)

*3. Terms and conditions*

*3.1. Data protection related content (Bullet point 16)*

*_„16. Persönliche Daten_*

# _Die Teilnehmer sind sich darüber bewusst, dass ihre persönlichen Daten, d. h. Identifikationsmerkmale, Adresse, Beruf und alle in den Dokumenten enthaltenen Elemente, in die Bolt-Datenbank aufgenommen und ausschließlich zum Zweck dieses Programms elektronisch verarbeitet werden._
# _Bolt schützt die personenbezogenen Daten der Teilnehmer und verwendet sie ausschließlich zur Durchführung dieses Programms unter Beachtung der geltenden allgemeinverbindlichen Rechtsvorschriften._
# _Die Richtlinien von Bolt zum Schutz personenbezogener Daten sowie die Regeln und der Umfang der Weitergabe personenbezogener Daten der Teilnehmer sind in der Bolt-Datenschutzerklärung dargelegt._
# _Als betroffene Personen haben die Teilnehmer mehrere Rechte in Bezug auf ihre personenbezogenen Daten, wie z. B. das Recht auf Auskunft und Information über die Verarbeitung personenbezogener Daten oder das Recht auf Löschung._
# _Weitere Informationen zum Datenschutz und zu den Rechten der Teilnehmer in Bezug auf die Verarbeitung ihrer personenbezogenen Daten findest du in der Bolt Global Privacy Policy, die unter_ [+_https://bolt.eu/en/legal/privacy-for-riders/_+|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/privacy-for-riders/] _abrufbar ist.“_

*Ad 1)* Data subjects are getting a misleading information about the collected data (address, jobs,...)

*Ad 3)* The terms and conditions refer to Bolt's privacy policy and data protection guidelines in connection with the transfer of data collected as part of the contest. However, there is currently no privacy notice for this group of addressees and this type of data processing (just riders, passengers, employees,…)

*Ad 4)* The most important data subject rights should also be listed here as part of a multi-layered privacy notice. In particular, there is no reference to the right to lodge a complaint.

 *Ad 5.)* The Bolt Global Privacy Policy deals with the processing activities related to user of the ride hailing-service. There are differences in the categories of data subjects, categories of data, the processing activity and the purpose. The link to the global policy for riders is misleading

*→ I would recommend using a separate privacy notice (provide link in the terms and conditions)*

*3.2. Additional Remarks*

When reviewing the „Allgemeine Geschäftsbedingungen“ (General Terms and Conditions), several inaccuracies in the German translation were noticed. The heading "Participants in the Program" can be mentioned here as an example, which was not translated into German at all.  Due to a lack of expertise, no final comments can be made here. 

*4. Use of Google-Forms*

Bolt is using a Googleforms-template for this campaign. In a decision, the Austrian Data Protection Authority ("Datenschutzbehörde" or "DSB") has decided on a model case that the continuous use of Google Analytics violates the GDPR. This is the first decision in the wake of the so-called "Schrems II" decision. In 2020, the Court of Justice (CJEU) decided that the use of US providers violates the GDPR, as US surveillance laws require US providers like Google or Facebook to provide personal details to US authorities. In late January, a Munich regional court ruled that a plaintiff was entitled to injunctive relief and damages of 100 € from an undisclosed website owner for passing on the visitor’s IP address to Google through the use of Google Fonts. Since it is possible to use the fonts without connecting to Google, the court deemed this a violation of Europe’s GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) because Google Fonts exposes the visitor’s IP address

*→ After the Schrems II decision and the current rulings of multiple data protection authorities regarding the usage of Google services I highly recommend to check if there are other privacy compliant options inside the European union (and use them).*

 *5. Who is the controller*

The GDPR defines the “controller” as the  natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data. The individual obligations and also the content depend on the respective controller function (Bolt Operations ÖU or Bolt Services DE GmbH).

→ *In order to determine who is the controller, it should be clearly defined in advance who is responsible for the action (who decides on the purpose and the chosen means or whether a contest is happening at all) (Bolt Operations ÖU or Bolt Services DE GmbH).*

*6. Additional requirements*

*6.1.  Safeguards*

While processing personal data, you also have to make sure, that proper safeguards are in place. That includes security by protecting the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the Personal Data, defined as follows:

*Confidentiality* means that only people who have a need to know and are authorised to use the Personal Data can access it.

*Integrity* means that Personal Data is accurate and suitable for the purpose for which it is processed.

*Availability* means that authorised users are able to access the Personal Data when they need it for authorised purposes.

*6.2.  Consent:*

* *Providing information*

Since Bolt also obtains the consent of the data subject before processing, the information provided in advance and the request for consent must be made in an understandable and easily accessible form using clear and plain language. For consent to be voluntary, the data subject must have a real choice. This requires adequate information.

If the consent is intended to legitimize the processing of personal data, the information must expressly refer to it. In any case, the data subject must be informed of the possibility of withdrawing their consent. (see Draft of the privacy notice)

*  *Obtaining Consent*

There is no formal requirement for consent, although written consent is still recommended due to the responsibility of the controller. They can therefore also take place in electronic form. Using an opt-in (in Germany I also would recommend a double-Opt-In) is a proper form. It also helps, documenting the given consent.

*  *Confirmation of consent/withdrawal of consent*

Participants of the “ditch your car”-campaign are not getting a confirmation of the application (no confirmation-mail). This makes it difficult for the data subject to withdraw their consent if necessary. Since a withdrawal should be just as easy as the consent itself, a confirmation e-mail with a withdrawal button is recommended.

*6.3.  Retention Period*

The collected personal data must be deleted by the controller (Bolt/Bolt subsidiary) and any processors after the end of the competition (or any statutory retention requirements).

*6.4.  purpose related processing*

The data may only be processed for the purpose for which they were collected (contest). Other purposes (newsletter, other marketing campaigns require their own legal basis)

*An update on Bolt Balance T&Cs:*

[Bolt Balance T&Cs|https://assets.ctfassets.net/tk7rwcciwvbq/2lgOlpDbGaWFvEtbOhBL5u/12150c515cc7f445e11a23fe816619d2/Bolt_Balance_Terms_and_Conditions__effective_as_of_31_March_2022_.pdf] will likely be launched at some point during April in each of the countries where we operate (never mind the Effective Date referred to in the link, this will be postponed). 

*What the Bolt Balance T&Cs provide in terms of refunds / compensation:*

Section 1.1.2 of the T&Cs will stipulate that amount on Bolt Balance may also be accrued as a result of us making refunds to Bolt Balance. This does not, however, mean that the Bolt Balance T&Cs would give us the contractual right to do refunds / compensation exclusively to Bolt Balance and even if they did, then this does not mean that applicable laws would not override such contractual right and allow us to do refunds / compensation exclusively to Bolt Balance. Most likely, applicable laws should be understood so as to leave users with the right to demand that refunds / compensation in cash no matter what we write in our T&Cs - i.e. by way of making a transfer to the user’s bank account or by rescinding a card payment. 

*How I think we should approach refunds / compensation:*

A transfer to the user’s bank account is something we cannot do by default as we do not know the user’s bank account number and it is something we probably do not want to do even if we did know the user’s bank account number as it involves a lot of manual labor and it includes transaction costs. Rescinding a card payment means that we have to refund the entire amount paid by the user as, because of technical reasons, there is no way to do a partial refund to the user’s card. 

Now therefore, I would suggest, that we do all partial refunds / compensations to Bolt Balance. If the user complains about it then we accept the risk that we may have breached applicable laws and trust that the user will not do anything about it as the amounts are rather small. For full refunds, we ask the user whether it is ok if we made the refund to Bolt Balance or whether the user necessarily wants a refund back to the user’s card and then do as instructed by the user. 

Note that if we do a refund to Bolt Balance, then, as it currently stands, because of technical reasons, there is no option for us to take back those amounts from Bolt Balance - for example in case we should want to opt for a full refund to the card instead. If we should one day develop the capacity to do that, then we could also consider taking a more aggressive with full refunds, where we make the full refund to Bolt Balance by default and if the user complains, then make a refund to the card and rescind the refund to Bolt Balance.

But these are only my thoughts and I think I do not have the mandate to decide how we handle refunds and compensation for our products. Thank you for your answer. From the perspective of the Swedish regulator and courts, a fixed price is to be understood as that the fixed price will not change depending on the customer's use of the service. While it is permissible to charge additional fees, these fees must be clearly described. 

Basically, if the customer books a ride for a fixed price of EUR 6,40, it should not come as a surprise for the customer if the final price exceeds EUR 6,40 and the customer should also understand the basis for why the final price is higher than the fixed price.

I do believe that our main challenge here is making the pricing understandable to the customer when booking the trip in the app. In regards to the website, my assessment is that we can refer to that the actual prices will be available in the app but it would be good if we at least can explain that the driver will set a price for the trip and that additional charges can occur in the event of tolls and changes in the route due to roadworks, closed roads/tunnels and car accidents etc.

Best regards,

Erik

Hey will wrap up this following all inputs received and propose action points + process guidelines (for now + long term vision):

*Refresher on the Legal Assessment*

The only truly compliant way to initiate user refunds (across all verticals) to Bolt Balance (instead of back to original payment method/bank-wire/cash) - is to seek for User’s consent to do this \[does not matter if its in-product consent or CS-acquired consent]. Anything short of that is open for legal challenges. 

Cannot contract out of this fully \[i.e. stating in T&Cs that refunds go to BB - likely unenforceable]

*_Why we can accept a consent-less refund process (for now)?_*

* scale of complaints triggered by refunds to BB - low
* amounts involved (AOV) - low 

Both factors above allow us to predict that we would be able to capture/handle the majority of the cases via CS interactions with users without them escalating into a legal issue.

*The proposed refund process for now* 

* *1st step* - *contractual “de-escalation”*: Bolt Balance T&Cs rolled out in all Bolt markets
** they do state Bolt’s right to initiate refunds to BB
* *2nd step - risk-adjusted refund process (*[~accountid:5d43ea3f1a6bf10be6db0f6e] [~accountid:5a9eaf7ca00c7f2a80156a09] ): 
** *Partial refunds* (all verticals): given the lack of ability to do partial refunds back to the original payment method (+additional expense to make bank-wire) we can set *_default rules to refund to BB_*
*** If user complaints: explain tech limitations to do partial refund back to or. payment method + point to BB T&Cs
*** If escalates further:
**** consider one-off bank wire (for partial amount) OR
**** accept the risk of user raising a legal issue with consumer bodies
** *Full Refunds* (all verticals)*:*
*** Track 1: assess the ability to *_add a CS-based consent step_* prior to initiating full-refund
**** _preferred long-term option_
*** Track 2: *_initiate refunds to Bolt Balance as default → send to OPM if escalated_*
**** IF user escalates/raises ticket: explain why the refund was done to BB (point to BB T&Cs) => BUT always immediately accept a request to refund back to the original payment method. 
* *3rd step - product/process adjustments (*[~accountid:610279833900e60070a347f0] [~accountid:5e99b13b34f7b90c0fcdb782] ):
** *Develop the ability to adjust Bolt Balance*: if the default is refunding to Bolt Balance, but a fall-back is refunding back to the original payment method, we need to be able to retroactively adjust Bolt Balance after refunds are done to the original payment method
** *Ability/process for making partial refunds via bank-wire:* to address user escalation around partial refunds going to BB without fall-back on back to OPM - it is worth exploring and setting up plan C in case the user insists on the non-BB partial refund. 

 This is a unified Refund-Process approach across all verticals. Detailed processes/instructions can be developed based on the above. Each vertical product counsel will support developing more granular / vertical-specific refund policies. [http://datascience.internal/data_hacks/ds-hometask/hometask-stats.html|http://datascience.internal/data_hacks/ds-hometask/hometask-stats.html]

Some conclusions:

* Hometask score is somewhat representative of candidate performance in the hiring pipeline. Candidates for whom we sent offer have higher scores compared to candidates who passed the hometask, but fail at some step.
* Performance in terms of section scores is also logical. Candidates who get the offer have avg scores higher for all hometasks section that candidates who just passed. Same relation between passed and not_passed.
* Biggest distinction between passed and offer candidates seems to lie in Solving the task section which implies that candidate who have better Product sense perform best further down the line.
* For not_passed candidates there is no clear pattern of what section drags them the most down. They seem to perform considerably worse on all the sections of the hometask.
* Our overall yearly* pass rate is similar between 2021 and 2022 years so far.
* There is considerable amount of hometasks which have the score a bit below the threshold (so 55-60 range), for some of those decision was to allow the candidate to proceed to the next stage.


Note 1: Year split is a bit skewed as 2022 data start from the end of February.
Note 2: Not all hometasks are present as some of the graders log their score outside of GoogleSheets Hiring Scoreards most of the team is using (2021 and 2022)
